strengths: The paper addresses a practically highly relevant problem: achieving decision-level sufficiency (predictive parity) from group-calibrated scores without assuming continuity or full support of the score distribution.
The geometric characterization of the feasible $(PPV, FOR)$ region for calibrated scores is elegant and mathematically rigorous.

The proposed post-processing algorithm (Algorithm 1) is exact, runs in polynomial time, and can optimize various objectives (such as expected loss or deviation from separation) along the boundary of the intersection region.
The theoretical proofs in the appendix are comprehensive, clear, and well-structured.
weaknesses: The empirical validation is quite limited, focusing only on a single, well-known dataset (COMPAS). Additional experiments on more datasets or synthetic simulations would help demonstrate the robustness of the estimator to sample size variations when estimating group-wise score distributions.

The distinction between score-level sufficiency (group calibration) and decision-level sufficiency (predictive parity) can sometimes be confusing in the literature; while the paper clarifies this in Section 2, the introduction could benefit from an earlier and sharper distinction.

The computational complexity of the boundary-tracing algorithm (which scales with the product of the number of unique score values in each group, $O(m^0 m^1)$) is not explicitly discussed, which is important when dealing with high-resolution scores.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and theoretically challenging problem: optimal binary classification satisfying sufficiency (predictive parity) when scores are finite-valued and group-calibrated.

Provides an elegant and precise geometric characterization of the feasible region in the PPV-FOR space, showing that the unconstrained feasible region is star-convex, which allows for piecewise-defined boundaries.

Introduces an efficient, exact post-processing algorithm (Algorithm 1) to trace the intersection boundary of subgroup feasible regions and find optimal classifiers under various objectives (e.g., expected loss, deviation from separation) by solving piecewise quadratic equations.
The writing is exceptionally clear, with well-structured proofs in the appendix and intuitive visualizations of the geometric concepts in the main text.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is limited to a single dataset (COMPAS) and a binary protected attribute. A more comprehensive empirical study showing the sensitivity of the method to finite-sample estimation of calibration and its scalability with respect to the number of score bins would make the paper stronger.

The method assumes perfect group-calibration of the input scores. In real-world applications, calibration must be estimated from data, and the paper does not deeply analyze how estimation errors or miscalibration affect the downstream fairness and utility guarantees.

While the authors claim that extending the method to more than two groups is straightforward, the complexity of finding the intersection of multiple (G > 2) star-convex regions is not discussed in detail.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly important and technically challenging problem in algorithmic fairness: achieving optimal binary classification under sufficiency (predictive parity) when dealing with finite-valued, group-calibrated scores.

The geometric characterization of the feasible region of (PPV, FOR) pairs as a star-convex set, and the characterization of the boundary of their intersection across groups, is elegant, rigorous, and theoretically sound.

The proposed post-processing algorithm (Algorithm 1) provides an exact and efficient way to trace the boundary and find the optimal classifier for various objectives, including loss minimization and minimizing deviation from separation.
The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, with clear explanations, illustrative figures (such as Figures 1 and 2), and comprehensive proofs provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is quite limited, as it is only demonstrated on a single dataset (COMPAS) with a basic 20/80 split. Testing on more benchmark datasets (e.g., Adult, German Credit) and comparing against alternative post-processing strategies would significantly strengthen the empirical claims.

The theoretical framework assumes that group-calibrated scores are already available or can be perfectly estimated. In practice, the finite-sample error of the calibration step can propagate to the downstream classification, and this sample complexity/robustness is not analyzed.

While the authors state that the extension to multi-group scenarios ($|A| > 2$) is straightforward, the algorithms and geometric analyses are presented almost exclusively for the binary group case. Tracing the boundary of the intersection of more than two regions is computationally and conceptually more complex, and a detailed discussion of this scalability is missing.

The optimal classifiers often rely on randomized decisions (as shown in Theorem 3.3). In real-world high-stakes domains (e.g., lending, criminal justice), randomized decision-making can face severe ethical, legal, and public acceptance hurdles, which deserves a more prominent discussion in the main text.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and realistic setting by focusing on finite-valued, group-calibrated scores rather than assuming continuous score distributions with full support.

Provides a strong and elegant theoretical foundation, geometrically characterising the feasible region of PPV and FOR, proving star-convexity, and deriving exact boundary curves using a fractional knapsack framework.

Derives a simple, exact, and computationally efficient post-processing algorithm (Algorithm 1) that traces the boundary of the intersection region to optimize arbitrary objectives (like expected loss or deviation from separation).

Includes a crucial robustness analysis establishing that predictive parity violations are bounded linearly by the maximum calibration error ($2\epsilon$), making the method reliable when scores are only approximately calibrated in practice.
The writing is exceptionally clear, and the figures (especially Figures 1 and 2) do a fantastic job of illustrating the underlying geometry of the intersection of feasible regions.
weaknesses: The scope of the paper is limited to binary classification and binary target variables; extensions to multi-class classification are not explored.

When the intersection of the subgroup-feasible regions is empty (which becomes more likely as the number of protected groups increases), the method is forced to fall back on degenerate or trivial classifiers.

The optimal sufficient classifiers require explicit access to the protected attribute $A$ at decision time (group-specific randomization rules), which may raise legal or policy concerns regarding disparate treatment in certain applications.

strengths: Addresses a crucial and challenging gap in algorithmic fairness: achieving optimal binary decisions under the 'sufficiency' (predictive parity) constraint using post-processing.

Formulates the problem in the highly practical setting of finite-valued, group-calibrated scores, which directly corresponds to how scores are used and stored in real-world systems (e.g., deciles, credit-score bins).

Provides an elegant and rigorous geometric characterization of the feasible region of PPV and FOR, proving star-convexity and showing that the optimal classifiers lie on the boundary of the intersection of group-specific feasible regions.
Develops an exact, efficient, and simple post-processing algorithm to find the optimal fair classifier for expected loss minimization or minimizing deviation from separation.

Includes a valuable robustness analysis showing that the predictive parity violation is bounded linearly by the group-calibration error ($2\epsilon$), ensuring the method is stable under approximate calibration.
The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, with highly clear explanations, illustrative figures, and comprehensive proofs in the appendix.
weaknesses: The optimal decisions often require randomized rules (soft thresholding). In high-stakes applications like lending or criminal justice, randomized decision-making can face significant ethical, legal, or practical hurdles, which deserves more discussion.

The analysis is primarily detailed for a binary protected attribute. While the extension to multiple groups is mentioned, the intersection of multiple feasible regions is much more likely to be empty, a limitation that could be discussed in greater detail regarding practical relaxations.

strengths: Novel and Elegant Geometric Framework: The paper introduces a novel star-convexity-based geometric characterization of the feasible (PPV, FOR) region for group-calibrated scores. This is a highly intuitive and mathematically rigorous way to handle the non-linear constraints of predictive parity, which are typically much harder to optimize than linear criteria like demographic parity or equalized odds.

Exact Solution for Practical Scenarios: Unlike prior works that rely on strong assumptions of continuous scores with full support, this work solves the practically relevant setting of finite-valued scores (e.g., binned credit scores or risk deciles) and provides an exact, non-heuristic algorithm.

Comprehensive Objective Optimization: The proposed framework is versatile. It can optimally minimize any standard classification loss under sufficiency (Section 5) as well as minimize the deviation from separation (Section 6), effectively addressing the well-known incompatibility between fairness definitions.

Thorough Theoretical and Empirical Validation: Detailed proofs are provided for all main results. The paper also includes a valuable robustness analysis under approximate calibration (with a proven $2\epsilon$ bound on fairness violation) and validates the findings on standard datasets (FICO, COMPAS, and ACS Income).
weaknesses: Use of Randomized Classifiers: The optimal sufficient decision rules often lie on the boundary of the intersection but in the interior of individual group regions, necessitating randomized predictions. In high-stakes domains (e.g., criminal justice or lending), randomized decisions based on a coin flip can be legally and ethically difficult to justify. More discussion on finding the best deterministic approximation would enhance the practical value.

Scalability to Multiple Groups: While the framework is presented for binary groups, extending to $K > 2$ protected groups means finding the intersection of $K$ distinct regions. The intersection of many such regions is much more likely to be empty or extremely small in practice, which limits the real-world applicability of exact sufficiency.

Baseline Comparisons: The empirical evaluation compares the proposed method primarily to the unconstrained baseline and the deviation-from-separation alternative. Including empirical comparisons with other existing heuristic or relaxation-based methods for enforcing predictive parity (e.g., Celis et al., 2019) would better highlight the utility and performance gap of the exact optimal solution.
